title: SDK Sprint Zero: playlist + hypotheses
body:
Purpose and scope:

This is a working note for a Sprint Zero (2-week) playbook: a compact set of experiments and quick wins to validate our assumptions about "ease of first successful SDK call" and the minimal surface area required for a delightful first 10 minutes. The goal is not to ship a complete product doc but to discover blockers, measure baseline metrics, and produce small, testable changes we can A/B in the playground and docs.

Intended audience:
- Developer experience engineers
- Docs writers
- SDK maintainers
- Solutions engineering (for pilot feedback)

High-level hypotheses (to validate in sprint):
1) Time-to-first-token (TTFT) is dominated by credential/config friction, not code complexity. If we reduce credential steps to a single env var + one-line CLI token fetch, TTFT will drop by >=50%.
2) A single opinionated quickstart (Node + Python) that includes a mini-app pattern (chat + retry fallback) will increase conversion from try-to-provision -> sample-success by >25% for new signups.
3) Error messages from initial SDK calls are too generic; a small set of contextualized errors + remediation suggestions will reduce support tickets for onboarding by 40%.
4) A runnable minimal project (30–80 LOC) that runs locally with a mocked local proxy will surface fewer infra-related questions during Sandbox trials.

Success criteria / measurement plan:
- TTFT: measure time between project creation (or sandbox token issue) and first successful generation request. Collect via telemetry events: onboarding.start, onboarding.first_call_success, onboarding.first_call_failure. Baseline: 12+ minutes (observed in user interviews). Target: <=5 minutes.
- Quickstart conversion: instrument quickstart step completions (open quickstart, run sample, get sample output). Track percentage of users who reach sample output.
- Support volume: track tickets with label "onboarding-sdk" and compare 30 days pre/post changes.
- Qualitative: 6 usability interviews during and after sprint.

Sprint playlist (week-by-week, with owners):
Week 0 (prep) - Aisha:
- Create trimmed quickstart text drafts for Node and Python (one file each, ~200–300 words).
- Setup telemetry events and dashboards (simple counts, TTFT histogram).
- Create a lightweight CLI helper: rwinf auth:init that stores token in RW_TOKEN env var. Keep implementation tiny (50 LOC).

Week 1 - Liam + Priya:
- Implement CLI helper in SDK repo, add to README callouts.
- Build a minimal sample app (chat echo with fallback) in Node (index.js ~60 LOC) and Python (app.py ~70 LOC). Keep as single-file runnable examples.
- Add a local proxy mock: small script that returns deterministic generation for predictable output (so docs can show expected output).
- Update quickstart page with one-line curl and SDK snippet, and expected output block to copy/paste.

Week 2 - Diego + Docs reviewer:
- Ship quick telemetry dashboard (TTFT funnel) and check data freshness.
- Create a small experiment: show contextual error messages vs baseline for 10% of new users (feature flag).
- Run 6 moderated usability sessions with new devs and iterate sample code.
- Draft follow-up microtasks for next sprint based on findings.

Experiment matrix (lite) - what to vary / how to measure:
- Credential friction: baseline (manual API key paste) vs CLI-token flow (rwinf auth:init). Measure TTFT.
- Quickstart length: single-file sample vs 3-file tiny app. Measure completion rate & time.
- Mocked vs real sandbox: Compare error volume and qualitative confusion.
- Error messaging: generic SDK error vs error with remediation hint and link to docs. Measure support tickets and completion.

Minimal quickstart outlines (copy-ready drafts)
- Node (opinionated):
  1) Install: npm i @redwood-inference/sdk
  2) Authenticate: rwinf auth:init  # copies token to env RW_TOKEN (or set RW_TOKEN=xxx)
  3) index.js: (single file)
     const { Redwood } = require('@redwood-inference/sdk');
     const r = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.RW_TOKEN });
     const out = await r.generate({ model: 'redwood-1-small', prompt: 'Say hello in 3 words' });
     console.log(out.text);
  4) Expected output snippet in docs (so users can verify success).

- Python (opinionated):
  1) pip install redwood-inference
  2) export RW_TOKEN="$(rwinf auth:init --print)"  # optional helper to store token
  3) app.py (single file):
     from redwood import Redwood
     r = Redwood(api_key=os.getenv('RW_TOKEN'))
     print(r.generate('Say hello in 3 words').text)

Known rough edges to watch for (notes):
- Long download/install steps (native wheel compilation) -> avoid by publishing simple pure-python wheel and minimal node deps for quickstart. If not possible, add prebuilt binaries on playground images.
- Proxy network errors when users are behind corp proxies; mock proxy helps but we should detect and surface "proxy" specific remediation.
- Rate limits: new users hit low-rate buckets and see 429s. Consider special pilot token with relaxed throttle for 10% of onboarding flows. Discuss with infra.

Error taxonomy for first-call errors (proposed):
- credential.missing -> "No token found. Run: rwinf auth:init or set RW_TOKEN=<token>."
- auth.invalid -> "Token invalid or expired. Re-run rwinf auth:init. If this persists, open support."
- network.proxy -> "Detected proxy connection issues. Try running with --proxy or see proxy troubleshooting doc: <link>"
- rate.limit -> "Usage limit reached. Try again in a minute or request a sandbox boost via playground."

Telemetry event plan (minimal):
- onboarding.start (user id, source: quickstart page)
- onboarding.cli_auth_initiated
- onboarding.sample_run_attempt (language, sample_id)
- onboarding.first_call_success
- onboarding.first_call_failure (error_code)
- quickstart.abandon (step_number)

Runbook for demos / solutions engineering pilots:
- Use the mocked proxy and expected-output snippets so demos never fail on network flakiness.
- Have a pre-created sandbox token for pilots with relaxed rate limits.
- Keep a troubleshooting checklist (token, proxy, rate-limit, dep install).

Open questions / decisions to make quickly:
- Do we enable a temporary onboarding rate-limit relax for new users? (ask infra/SRE)
- Where should the CLI helper live? Monorepo cli-tools or each SDK package? (pref: centralized tiny repo)
- Which model(s) to use in quickstart for consistent runtimes and small output tokens (redwood-1-small vs redwood-chat-small)?

Next steps (immediate):
- Aisha: finalize the Node and Python single-file sample draft and post to #devex for quick review (today).
- Liam: spike CLI helper and open MR with README integration (48h).
- Priya: wire the minimal telemetry events into analytics sandbox and build the TTFT dashboard (end of week 1).

Notes to self (short):
- Keep examples minimal, avoid advanced features (tools, streaming) in first-run flows.
- Make expected outputs deterministic via mock so docs can include exact text to assert success.
- Capture both quantitative (TTFT) and qualitative (session notes) signals.

Attachments / copyable snippets: (for quick paste into README)
- Single-file Node example (index.js) and expected output block (3-word greeting)
- Single-file Python example (app.py) and expected output block
- One-liner CLI commands to set RW_TOKEN and test the SDK call

End of note.

-- Aisha
